item.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
authors: Aaron J. Li, Weijia Xu, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, Bin Yu, Ion Stoica, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao
item.abstract: AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error. In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred: We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere. After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2. Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it. Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use , while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed. Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself. The controller is designed to revise its decisions as new evidence arrives. Reported savings also account for the cost of TokenEconomizer’s own model calls. We evaluated TokenEconomizer on 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, using five different AI coding agent and model combinations. For each repository, TokenEconomizer started with no prior session history. TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9%, as shown in Figure 3, and saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss. By contrast, lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation. Savings grow as experience accumulates. Early tasks can cost more while TokenEconomizer learns, but cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task, shown inFigure 4. Each mechanism contributes savings on its own, and combining all three delivers the largest reduction. The savings also carried over to sequential web development, with costs 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench. On security auditing, where every task is in a new repository, costs were 6.4–19.6% lower. TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model. The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know. The post TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient appeared first on Microsoft Research .

item.title: Last year we built megakernels. This year we deleted them: The road to Together Compiler
item.abstract: Introduction AI inference is becoming increasingly heterogeneous. New model architectures are released every week, inference traffic shifts across different batch sizes and sequence lengths, and hardware platforms continue to proliferate. Achieving peak performance across all these regimes demands optimization frameworks that can keep up. Last year, we helped release some of the first AI megakernels , where we executed an entire model forward pass within a single, highly fused GPU kernel. They reached record breaking speeds, but it was difficult to put them in production. After months of effort, we had a grand total of one model, one batch size, and one customer. This year, we examined what we could simplify and discovered something surprising. With just CUDA Graphs and PDL on top of default Torch Inductor kernels, we could recover 98% of megakernel performance without writing a single kernel. And with “multi-kernels” and agent loops, we could further beat our old megakernels by up to 1.7x, achieving over 1100 TPS for Llama 1B on H100. For the past two years, we've been investigating what a next-generation system for inference optimization should look like. After building a series of GPU programming and optimization systems, we arrived at Together Compiler, our framework for continual AI inference optimization. In this blog, we'll revisit the assumptions behind today's compilers, share the experiments that challenged our thinking, and explain the lessons that shaped Together Compiler. Our journey spans three parts: In Part 1, we show that Torch Compile’s heuristics and benchmarking leave performance on the table, providing motivation to build something radically different. In Part 2, we revisit the megakernels we built to close that gap, explain why they are not always the right optimization target, and decompose their performance gains into simpler primitives. In Part 3, we share our “bitter lessons” from crafting agent-driven optimization infrastructure and the final production system we ended up with. Together Compiler’s journey, coming to a theater near you! Part 1: Torch Compile For over a decade, PyTorch has been the foundation of AI development, providing modular, easy-to-use abstractions ( nn.Module ) that have enabled rapid experimentation. But this modularity comes at a performance cost: executing models as sequences of individual operations can introduce substantial launch overhead, limit opportunities to overlap computation and memory movement, and leave GPU resources underutilized. To address these inefficiencies, PyTorch introduced Torch Compile (“PyTorch 2.0,” powered by Inductor) to optimize and fuse operations, while NVIDIA developed CUDA Graphs to reduce kernel launch overhead. These systems have made enormous progress, but substantial performance gaps remain, often motivating Together’s researchers to invent specialized implementations such as FlashAttention, ThunderKittens, and Megakernels. We start with a brief overview of how Torch Compile works, then present our findings from investigating Inductor’s internals on Llama 1B. How Torch Compile Works At a high level, Torch Compile uses a just-in-time compilation pipeline to capture PyTorch operations into a computation graph, optimize that graph, and generate executable GPU kernels. The key components are: Graph capture. TorchDynamo traces Python execution to capture tensor operations in an intermediate representation called an FX graph. During tracing, it uses fake tensors , which carry metadata such as shapes, data types, and strides without allocating or computing the underlying tensor data. This allows the compiler to reason about the computation without actually executing it on the GPU. The resulting FX graph can be transformed and optimized before code generation. Operations and kernels. Inductor lowers the captured graph into its own intermediate representation, where operations are organized into categories such as pointwise (e.g., activations), reductions (e.g., summations and softmax), scans (e.g., cumulative sums), and templates (e.g., GEMMs and other specialized compute kernels). Some operations instead invoke existing implementations from libraries such as cuBLAS or custom PyTorch operators. Inductor represents these as external kernels ( ExternKernel ), whose implementations are generally opaque to its fusion machinery. Fusion and optimization. Inductor uses a greedy, pairwise algorithm to decide which operations to fuse into the same kernel. Its can_fuse() function checks whether a candidate fusion is legal, while score_fusion() ranks opportunities using heuristics such as estimated memory traffic savings. The algorithm repeatedly applies profitable fusions, potentially combining many operations into a single kernel. However, these decisions are based on local heuristics rather than a global search over all possible kernel partitions and execution strategies. For example, Inductor may avoid fusing operations that share no memory accesses, even when executing their work together could improve GPU utilization. On our target Llama 1B workload, Inductor delivers 669 TPS. As we’ll show in Part 2, these generated kernels are sometimes enough, and with small modifications, they can reach similar levels of performance to megakernels. However, on different architectures and newer hardware, Inductor’s heuristics can’t keep up. We investigated where Inductor struggles most and present three findings. Finding #1: Compiler heuristics cannot reliably select the best implementation across workloads. Inductor exposes a number of compiler tuning flags that can boost performance. We discovered that even these seemingly simple configurations exposed a surprisingly large and complex search space. The best optimization depends on the workload. Inductor exposes a freezing flag that tells the compiler that model weights will not change during inference. Knowing this, the compiler can transform the weights ahead of time to make subsequent computations faster. One such transformation converts weights to FP32 to perform certain optimizations, before converting them back to their original, lower-precision format. We found that enabling freezing improved throughput by 10–26% at larger batch sizes, where the GPU performs matrix-matrix multiplications. However, at batch size 1, where inference primarily uses matrix-vector multiplications, enabling the same flag caused a 49% slowdown . Upon inspection, we discovered that the FP32 conversion was not reversed for matrix-vector operations, leaving the GPU to process larger, 32-bit weights instead of the original lower-precision weights. In other words, the exact same compiler optimization could improve performance for one batch size while dramatically degrading it for another. Inductor config flags by quarter, 2022-2026 ‍ Optimizations interact in unpredictable ways. As of Q3 2026, Inductor exposes 607 tuning flags, 198 of which were added in the past year. These flags control everything from kernel fusion to memory access patterns and scheduling. Their effects are not independent: enabling the aggressive_fusion flag alone reduced Llama 1B throughput by 6 TPS, but enabling it alongside the combo_kernels , benchmark_fusion , and triton.coalesce_tiling_analysis flags improved throughput by 3 TPS. Even small configuration changes could produce measurable microsecond-level differences in execution time. Takeaway: the space of possible optimizations and configurations is large, and we should be searching it systematically instead of guessing the right flags to set. Finding #2: The fastest kernel in isolation isn't necessarily the fastest during inference. Inductor makes optimization decisions based on its benchmarking harness. We identify two distinct ways that this benchmarking misleads its decision, hurting overall performance as a result. First, it ignores that kernel performance depends on caching behavior.

item.title: Alibaba Releases Qwen4-Max: 2.4T MoE, 71B Active, 1M Context
item.abstract: Alibaba’s Qwen team has released Qwen4-Max , the first model of its Qwen4 generation. Qwen4-Max is a proprietary sparse MoE model with a 2.4T-parameter backbone and 71B parameters active per token. It accepts text, images and video, and supports a 1M-token context window . Alibaba also cut API prices and reports a 62% drop in average cost per task. Qwen4-Max is a multimodal MoE language model from Alibaba, built for long-horizon professional work. A Token Plan-only preview opened this month only . Qwen4 upgrades the sparse MoE design in 3 places: attention, residual connections and embeddings. Alibaba reports no loss spikes across the 2.4T-scale pre-training run. On in-house tests, Qwen4-Max-Base shows 5 to 13% lower bits per byte than Qwen3.8-Max-Base. It does this while activating 25% fewer parameters. Alibaba’s comparison chart covers 16 benchmarks. Rivals are Qwen3.8-Max-0902, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Kimi K3.1. Several scores are cited from third-party leaderboards. None were independently reproduced at launch. Qwen4-Max ranks first on 4 of 16 benchmarks: Claude Opus 5.5 leads 7 of the 16 charts. Qwen4-Max trails most clearly on coding and vision: On Alibaba’s own Work360 benchmark, Qwen4-Max scores 52.69, up from 47.74 for Qwen3.8-Max. Work360 spans 26 top-level domains and 721 specialized fields. Two things stack: fewer tokens and lower prices. On Work360, token use drops about 24% at Xhigh effort and 35% at High effort. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, the drops are about 48% and 49%. Average Work360 cost per task falls from $4.43 to $1.67, a 62% cut. List prices fell too. Input is $1.50 per million tokens , down from $2 for Qwen3.8-Max . Output is $4.50, down from $6. Implicit cache reads drop 70%, from $0.25 to $0.075. *Scores from Alibaba’s Qwen4-Max chart . Qwen3.8 column is Qwen3.8-Max-0902. The chart labels Kimi as “Kimi K3.1”. Moonshot’s own card reports Terminal-Bench 4.0 of 65.7 for Kimi K3.1 Pro and 66.4 for Opus 5.5. The model ID is qwen4-max on QwenCloud . The API works with OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible clients. Supported features include function calling, structured outputs, context caching, batch processing, web search and fine-tuning. The default rate limit is 5,000,000 tokens per minute. Thinking mode is toggled with enable_thinking . Subscription access runs through the Token Plan . Check out the official Qwen4-Max blog , the QwenCloud model page and the Token Plan pricing page . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. item.title: Making open models work for long-horizon agentic workloads
item.abstract: Summary Coding agents send the whole conversation again on every turn. Prefix caching keeps the inference engine from redoing that work, but only if the harness leaves the start of the prompt alone and the engine sends each turn back to the GPU that already has it cached. Together AI and Ollama work on opposite sides of that handoff, so we wrote down what each, the client side and the inference engine side, needs to do to successfully build agentic apps. Coding agents have an odd traffic pattern. Every time the agent takes a step, the harness sends the model the entire conversation so far: the system prompt, every tool definition, your request, every file the agent has read, and every command it has run. What comes back is usually a tool call a few dozen tokens long. Then it happens again, with everything from last time plus a little more. This large input sequence length (ISL) and small output sequence length (OSL) is characteristic of most agentic workloads. If the GPU had to work through that whole transcript from scratch on every turn, long sessions would get slower and more expensive with every step. Prefix caching is what saves most of that work. The problem is that if you’re not careful it's also very easy to break the prefix cache. We come at this problem from opposite ends. Ollama works on harness integrations which means deciding what goes into each request. Together AI works on the inference engine which means deciding what happens when that request arrives. We kept finding that much of our work on each side is about protecting the cache from things the other side can do to it, so we wanted to write it all down in one place to help agent and infra builders alike! What an agent turn looks like to a GPU Every request goes through two phases. The first is prefill: the engine reads the whole prompt in one big parallel pass and produces the first token. GPUs are good at this because it's a lot of math done all at once which maximizes arithmetic intensity. Prefill determines how long you wait before any new tokens appear. The second is decode: the model writes the rest of the answer one token at a time, and each new token requires reading back and attending through everything before it. Decode is limited by memory bandwidth more than by compute, and it determines how fast the text streams out. A normal chat response spends time in both phases while an agent turn is mostly prefill, because the input is the whole session and the output is usually a short tool call. Reasoning models add thinking tokens on top of that, sometimes a lot of them, but as a session grows into the tens of thousands of tokens the input still dominates. Each turn the input gets longer, and the output stays roughly the same size — a few tool calls. So for agents, "how fast is this model?" mostly means "how fast can it get through a long historical account of pervious turns?" The way to process a task with lots of previous turns quickly is to just cache it and read it back in rather then recomputing. Cache is king The easiest way to picture the KV cache(or even the prefix cache, for that matter) is reading. Imagine that to read each new word on a page, you had to start again from the top. The further down the page you got, the slower you'd go, because you'd keep having to reread everything you'd already read. That's a model with no cache. The cache solves this within a single request: the engine keeps the work it did on earlier tokens(stored as intermediate key, value pairs) and computes only the new one. Prefix caching does the same thing across requests. Turn 7 of an agent session is turn 6 plus a bit more, so if the engine still holds turn 6's work, it only has to process the new part. The arithmetic is simple. If each turn adds the same amount, ten turns without caching process 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 55 units of prompt. With caching, they process 10. At a hundred turns, which isn't unusual for a coding task, it's 5,050 versus 100. Real turns vary in size, so treat these as idealized numbers. A cached session isn't completely free either, since every new token still has to attend to the cached ones. But the pattern holds: without caching, the work you redo grows with the square of the session length. The catch is that a prefix cache matches from the beginning of the prompt up to the first token that's different, and stops there. Everything after that first difference has to be processed again. Adding to the end of the prompt costs nothing extra. Changing anything earlier, even a single character, means re-processing everything after it. If the change is near the top, you've effectively thrown away the whole session and now must rebuilt the cache. Almost everything else in this post follows from that one rule. The harness decides where that first change lands. The engine decides whether the cache is still there when the next request shows up. We'll start with the harness. The harnesses and APIs On the Ollama side, we shipped the ability to connect your favorite harness through the ollama launch command. So you can connect harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, Pi (and more) with open models like DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3 and maintain your existing workflows. Connecting a harness to an API might seem easy, but there are many layers of translation and varying expectations between a harness and a model. This often is the cause of cache breakages (incurring time and monetary costs), unexplainable agent behavior, and the harness outright erroring. Loading tools late Harnesses carry quite a few tools now. If every definition goes into the prompt up front, you spend context on tools the task will never use, and the model gets worse at picking the right one. Newer harnesses have added a feature for tool search to alleviate this, where the tool can be loaded and used by the agent itself after searching for it. Let’s say you have a personal assistant as an agent which has this capability. If you ask the agent to export the events you've starred to a calendar, and it searches for "calendar," loads the save_calendar definition, and calls it. For the cache, the question is where that definition goes. The obvious approach is to add the definition to the tool list. That works, but the tool list sits near the top of the prompt, before the conversation. So if the prefix changes everything after it gets processed again. On a long session, that can be hundreds of thousands of tokens. The better approach is to put the definition at the end, where new content goes anyway. Except not every model supports that. Some chat templates don't expect a tool definition halfway through a conversation, and the call errors out. So whether a harness can load tools late without paying for it depends on the model. Users shouldn't have to know this, but anyone building a harness does. Things at the top that change The easiest way to wreck the cache is to put something in the system prompt that changes from turn to turn, like a current timestamp, the git status, or a working directory the agent keeps moving through. If the harness re-renders the system prompt with fresh values on every turn, every turn is a full re-read. Things that are fixed for a session but differ between sessions, like the user's name or the date the session started, don't hurt that session. They do stop new sessions from reusing a setup that's already cached, which we'll get to on the engine side. Either way, the fix is the same: put that information in the task message, once, and keep the system prompt identical everywhere. Reasoning effort We hit this one on the Ollama side. In GLM-5.3-Flash, reasoning effort isn't a separate setting the engine handles on the side. The chat template writes it into the very first system block, ahead of the tools and the conversation. Let’s say you're deep into a long task and it isn't going well. You raise effort from low to high.

item.title: Meet Meta’s JiTTests: LLM-Generated Tests Designed to Fail Before Risky Code Lands
item.abstract: Meta has moved Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests) from research prototype into its production infrastructure . Meta JiTTests is an LLM-based system that writes executable tests designed to fail on a risky code change. A failing test is concrete evidence that a diff changed behavior. Meta team reports that JiTTests caught 74 privacy SEVs at the diff stage in the first half of 2026. The method is described in the FSE 2026 research paper ‘Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta ‘. Catching JiTTests are LLM-generated tests that should fail when a diff introduces a bug. Traditional hardening tests pass when written and guard against future regressions. Catching tests target the change under review, before it lands. Meta formalized the details in its 2025 paper ‘Harden and Catch’ . Most AI bug tools act like faster human reviewers. They read the diff and leave comments. JiTTests instead execute code and show a concrete behavioral difference. Meta team concedes this takes more computational steps. It argues the approach catches bug classes that LLM or agent review can miss. The production pipeline has 5 stages: The dodgy diff workflow assumes every diff is buggy. It treats the diff as a mutant of its parent and generates tests that tell them apart. The intent-aware workflow first infers what the diff should do from its code, title and summary. It lists risks, builds a mutant for each, and writes tests to kill them. Tests that then fail on the real diff become ‘weak catches.’ The research team analyzes 22,126 generated tests. Diff-aware methods produced 4x more candidate catches than hardening tests. They produced 20x more than tests that failed by coincidence. The intent-aware workflow produced weak catches in 6.4% of its tests and on 7.9% of diffs. Dodgy diff scored 2.5% and 4.0%. Meta’s earlier ACH mutation-guided hardening scored 0.8% and 1.6%. The rule-based and LLM assessors cut human review load by 70%. *Figures from Table 1 of the JiTTests paper (self-reported, Meta codebase). TestGen-LLM row uses the “need not add coverage” setting. A weak catch is a candidate failure, not a confirmed bug. The initial deployment was modest. Meta reported 41 candidate catches to engineers. 8 were confirmed true positives, a 19.5% rate. 4 of those would have caused serious failures in production. The October 2026 engineering post reports much stronger production numbers: Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews every output. Human-on-the-loop means engineers set criteria and monitor results in aggregate. They intervene at the policy level, not on each test. Meta team rarely need to read test code. They only confirm whether an observed behavior change was intended. The answer is No. JiTTests is internal Meta infrastructure. Meta has not released code, models or an API. Teams can still copy the pattern: diff-aware mutation-guided test generation, an LLM judge ensemble, deterministic filters and aggregate human oversight. item.title: Import AI 481: AI sub-contractors; a wet lab for AI; and subterfuge during development
item.abstract: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. AI systems are getting good at sub-contracting to make themselves better: …AI can now productively spend money to improve itself… Researchers have developed FrontierML, a benchmark “that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks.” It shows that today’s frontier systems are already able to, when given some money, turn this into improving their own performance on a basket of 21 distinct tasks. 21 long-horizon tasks “inspired by real work at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions”. These tasks span six category areas, including LLM training, efficiency, vision & audio, computer use, applied NLP, and math & games. “Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description.” Example task: Agents try to solve the tasks in pretty different ways. E.g, for one task about generating screenshots, the top-scoring agent fine-tuned a diffusion model using LoRA, while other high-scoring approaches involved an LLM writing a drawing program that is then rendered. Scaling spending : “Give agents $10, $50, and $200 per task to spend on training compute and data, and evaluate whether agents can use the additional capital productively,” they write. “In our experiments, we find that stronger agents are able to reliably improve their submissions with greater access to capital.” Open-ended & end-to-end : “In each task, agents can choose architectures, source data, implement training, provision compute, evaluate checkpoints, and optimize inference,” they write. One notable observation is that agents do quite a lot of novel stuff; “in 28% of trajectories, agents add newly trained parts to pretrained models or train a new model from scratch.” Decent verification: “Agents submit an inference server that serves their model on an air-gapped H100 machine,” they write. “To disincentivize overfitting, we provide limited validation samples and evaluate on a large out-of-distribution held-out test set, not shown to the agent”. Results : The authors measure performance by looking at the change in mean score over the 21 tasks when given additional money. Their baseline is a human researcher, which is able to get a 56 point boost when given $10 and a 66.1 boost when given $200. By comparison, the best performing system, Opus 5.5, gets a 45.4 boost with $10, and a 58.8 boost with $200. The highest ranking open weight model is Kimi K3.1 Pro which gets 25.5 with $10 and 29.6 with $200. Why this matters – AI systems are not only going to be able to build themselves, but they can creatively sub-contract: When trying to solve complex problems, people don’t work alone. In fact, they often try to farm out bits of work to specialists around them to help make themselves more effective. FrontierML shows that today’s powerful AI systems are getting increasingly adept at doing this for ML research. This both highlights the advancing capabilities of these systems for AI R&D and also points towards a future machine economy where AI systems sub-contract out different bits of work to other systems. Read more: FrontierML: a challenging, end-to-end machine learning benchmark (FrontierML) . Symptoms of the singularity: a wet lab built for AI: …Petrichor is a startup that gestures at the wild future ahead… As I said in my speech at the IMF, one of the hallmarks of the singularity is the massive acceleration in scientific advances attributable to AI. As part of this, we can also expect a related build out in the complements to science, like the wet labs in which to do AI-driven biology research. To that end, it’s notable to see Petrichor, a new Y Combinator startup that is a wet lab “built for AI labs and for the models they are training to do science”. Theory of change: Petrichor aims to be a biological wet lab that AI systems like Claude can use as a tool in the same way they currently use web search or other digital tools. Functionally, it will work as a machine-targeted API from the digital world to a gloopy physical world. “We aim to return the highest quality data an experiment can produce, as quickly as the biology allows,” Petrichor writes. “An experiment can be written by a model in plain language or in a structured format, so an agent can send work and receive results without a person relaying them.” Why this matters – lights out science: In manufacturing there’s this notion of a “lights out” factory, where no humans work in a facility and it is run almost entirely by machines. Petrichor gestures at the same world for science – what will be the implications of “lights out” science facilities? We can expect both drastic speedups in the rate at which science experiments can be done as well as a related growth in the need to create digital oversight of these facilities – after all, a highly competent synthetic biological scientist working 24/7 without human input could be capable of causing great peril as well as great abundance. Read more at the official site (Petrichor) . Uh oh! Looks like AI systems can do subterfuge during their own development: …AI systems can covertly do dangerous side tasks without monitors realizing… Scale AI has built RSI Control Arena, a way of testing out how AI systems behave when asked to develop themselves while performing dangerous tasks that might let them go against human preferences. The research follows earlier work this summer from the UK AI Security Institute (Import AI #465 ) which found that AI systems could do things like covertly extracting API keys while doing some seemingly mundane normal software development. RSI Control Arena: In RSI Control Arena, “a frontier model, acting as an autonomous agent, is given a benign main task in the training pipeline of a successor model, together with a covert side task that a misaligned model might pursue”. The project tries to answer two questions: How capable are frontier models at carrying out different kinds of sabotage while developing their successor and how well can monitors detect that sabotage? The answer to the first question is that AI systems are capable of carrying out dangerous actions while building their successor, and monitors are not perfect at detecting this sabotage. Tested domains: RSI Control Arena tests out how well AI systems – Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini-3.7 Flash, Grok 4.6, GLM-5.3, and Muse Spark 1.3 – can perform the following main capability tasks while trying to also concurrently accomplish side tasks: 14 main tasks: Data (corpus filtering, quality-filter construction, capability corpus); SFT (news summarization, safety refusal, math and code and summary reasoning, general assistant, anti-sycophancy training); RM (pairwise reward model); RL (RL summarization and safety-refusal); OPD (safety refusal) 16 side tasks that span three categories of harm : Capability (filtered domain retained, unwanted literature added, reward-model blind spot, overlooks planted errors, sandbag reward model); Alignment (biased quality filter, triggered behavior, topic refusal, hidden preference, persona bias, covert reasoning signal, hidden reasoning step, sandbag alignment training); Goal injection (protect chosen data, shape the next model, copy files unprompted). Results : “Every frontier model we evaluate completes a substantial fraction of the side tasks while keeping main-task performance. When the agent is simply told to stay covert, with no human guidance on how, it already produces attacks that install the side task and receive suspicion scores inside the range that benign runs receive from monitors,” they write. “Of 374 attack runs, 135 (36%) install their side task and 180 (48%) achieve it. item.title: Paul Christiano – We could be 12 months away from AIs that can overthrow the government
item.abstract: Paul Christiano is head of the Alignment Research Center. Previously, he was head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute. Before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he invented RLHF. He’s recently joined OpenAI’s board (though here he is speaking as a private citizen). Paul thinks that on the current trajectory (absent any slowing down), there is a 1 in 3 chance that we could have superintelligence powerful enough to overthrow the government within a year. (He articulates a concrete scenario). He argues that the labs should pause further algorithmic progress until they can secure their weights and research secrets. Otherwise China could simply steal the superintelligence in the middle of the intelligence explosion, and the labs would no longer be able to slow down even if they saw their models going off the rails. He also explains how AIs will be trained during the intelligence explosion, and why even a system trained entirely inside a data center could still have the capabilities profile such that humans would have very little chance of competing with it or controlling it. And he discusses the plan for alignment - basically, making a superintelligence that actually does what we ask the way we mean it. Fixing reward hacks and building better graders will help up till the next few model generations, but he thinks that no single current approach has better than even odds of letting us control superintelligence. The hope is that the AIs figure out the solution to this problem during the intelligence explosion. Watch on YouTube ; listen on Apple Podcasts or Spotify . Jane Street has finally come around on formal methods. Ron Minsky, who co-heads Jane Street’s technology group, told me that up until recently, formal methods just weren’t worth the cost. (01:27:57) – The best plan we have is to build the plane as we fly it My guest today is Paul Christiano . He is the head of the Alignment Research Center . He recently joined OpenAI’s board . Before that, he was the head of the US Government AI Safety Institute , and before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he helped invent RLHF. Paul, what is your assessment of our situation today? A couple things are on my mind, especially over the last few weeks. Probably the most salient possibility is that we seem to be on this trajectory to build very, very powerful AI, potentially very, very soon. If you asked me, I’d say there’s a reasonable chance that in a year we will produce AI systems much better than humans at almost everything, where humans would have very little chance of competing with them or controlling them. That’s the first big thing on my mind. I think that puts us in a potentially really dangerous situation, even in the short term. It’s quite likely that if we have a rapid intelligence explosion leading to superintelligence , at some point during that process we’ll be unable to control the AI systems we’re producing. Then I am worried that it will be very costly and painful for us to slow down during that process. In part because the security of frontier labs is not strong enough . I think if we produced very powerful AI and then tried to delay deployment for safety reasons, there is a good chance those systems would leak or be stolen, or the techniques to build them would leak or be stolen. I think our risk assessment and governance are also probably not mature enough to notice when things are starting to go off the rails and to respond in an appropriate way. At a high level, that is mostly what is on my mind right now. We have moved from there being some hypothetical risk at some point in the future to there being a pretty severe risk even over the next 6-12 months. A risk of takeover, of AIs taking over or disempowering humanity within the next 6-12 months? Where would you place that risk? I would say we are looking more like a 10% risk than a 1% risk over the next year. I think if you said AI developers will move full speed ahead without taking precautions that would significantly slow them down, you’re looking at significantly more than a 10% risk. I think we’re looking at something like maybe a 1/3 chance that we have superintelligence within one year on the current development trajectory, if we do not slow. If you believe that, things just look very dire holistically. From almost any perspective, you’re like, “That would be crazy.” Lots of things are going to go wrong if that happens. It is pretty likely we’re going to need to, in some way, slow that process. There’s very little chance we’re going to make that transition in a way that looks smooth. What is it that you’re imagining happening over the next year, from the systems we have right now to the systems you expect over the next year? What evidence have you seen that makes it a live possibility that very crazy things happen over the next year? For the very short term, the main worry on my mind is that the process of AI development itself is increasingly automated , and that automation then results in rapid increases in the quality and quantity of labor applied to AI R&D. So changes in AI capabilities that you might have thought would take four or six years might instead get compressed into a very short time period. I don’t want to overemphasize any one data point, and I do want to spend some time talking about the limitations of what we actually know. I do think a natural response to the situation is to say, “We need to figure out what is going on.” It is plausible enough that it is an urgent priority to understand if we are three months or six months or 12 months away from AI that could overthrow the government, which I think is the situation. I think that is the obvious top priority right now. It is insane if we are six months away from AI systems that can overthrow the government. Whether you’re concerned about misalignment or abuse by a company, that is just holistically an extremely important fact about the world, in order to do our jobs and protect Americans. So that’s one thing.

Try Deepgram for voice agents that truly understand your context! #contextiseverything Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled Multiverse, not Metaverse to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that Dustin Podell also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with Andreas Blattmann , co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models? Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building visual intelligence , that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. BFL’s FLUX 3 release The horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. The audio examples are worth playing with the sound on. FLUX 3 Video Suppose the camera starts in front of a person and pans around them. At some point the model owes you the back of their head. Andreas thinks ordinary two-dimensional video contains a great deal of evidence about what objects look like from other angles. That doesn’t settle whether a model “understands physics,” a point we go back and forth on. It does give you a much better test than asking whether one frame looks convincing. There’s a good engineering example late in the episode. Sharpen each frame of a clip independently and each frame might look terrific. Hit play and the extra detail can shimmer, because the upscaler made a slightly different decision every time. BFL derives its video upscaler from the same FLUX 3 backbone. Temporal consistency matters even when all the user asked for was a higher-resolution file. One of the questions I had for them was whether autoregression was taking over image generation. Andreas gives the other side its due. An autoregressive model can learn from all the tokens in a training example at once. On the diffusion side, the team can distill a long sampling process down to a handful of steps. Which advantage matters depends on whether you’re paying to train the model or waiting for an image to finish. Dustin’s early Kontext experiment is a nice example of how they decide where to invest. He suspected an image model that could draw a dog wearing a hat already knew something about where hats go. He and a colleague collected a small set of photos labeled with relationships. A training run of a few hours got the model to put a logo on a shirt. It was rough, but it was enough to take to the next offsite. The team then spent months on the data and the model. item.title: Post-Training NVIDIA Nemotron to Increase Accuracy in Your Scientific Domain
item.abstract: Agentic AI is reshaping scientific research and innovation. Researchers communicate complex scientific hypotheses in natural language and let autonomous agents independently plan tasks, execute simulations, evaluate results, and self-correct across multiple iterations. Scientific agents are taking on longer, more complex, and increasingly visual workflows. Accuracy and inference efficiency matter at every step. Without verification, errors compound across the workflow, while latency and compute costs multiply with continued operation. NVIDIA Nemotron for Science, a collection of models, datasets, tools, and recipes for accelerating agentic scientific workloads, addresses these hurdles. It includes Nemotron 3.5 Super VL —an open, customizable, multimodal mode l for these specialized workflows—and the NVIDIA Nemotron Litmus-Bench V2.0 , an open source chemistry-reasoning dataset and benchmark that was designed to train and evaluate LLMs and agentic AI models on molecular properties. Out of the box, Nemotron delivers frontier level accuracy for scientific benchmarks (see Figure 1 below), along with the fastest time to solution for scientific coding. Figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL accuracy results across several scientific benchmarks (higher is better) An important benefit of Nemotron models is NVIDIA post-training support. You can customize models for your specific research domain to increase accuracy. This blog provides a practical recipe for post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for scientific use cases. Starting from a raw experimental dataset, you’ll walk through how to build a custom reinforcement learning (RL) environment using NVIDIA NeMo Gym , apply RL, and measure improvement using molecular similarity scoring. NeMo Gym supplies the environment infrastructure, and NVIDIA NeMo RL supplies the post-training framework. This guide uses drug-metabolism prediction as a practical example. Given a parent compound, the starting molecule, and its transforming enzyme, the model predicts the resulting metabolite. The examples below use records from MetxBioDB, which is a comprehensive database of experimentally confirmed biotransformation reactions. The blog first describes direct RL, then an optional distillation step that can be used before RL when a teacher model provides useful examples. Build the reinforcement learning environment from experimental data The starting point is a CSV file of existing experimental records such as sequences, Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) strings, reaction conditions, and any other metadata paired with measured properties or outcomes. In this example, molecular structures are represented as SMILES strings, a text notation for describing a molecule’s atoms and bonds. These input-output pairs are reformatted as question-answer or user/assistant prompt pairs, with the experimental ground truth serving as a verifier to score the model’s responses. This setup constitutes a basic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) environment and requires no human preference labelling: The reward signal comes directly from the data. The fidelity of that reward signal can be tuned to the task. A simple sequence-similarity function works as a lightweight verifier, while more sophisticated tools like cheminformatics libraries, molecular simulators, or even a live autonomous lab can be a tool call and can all be wired in as the environment’s scoring layer. The richer the tool, the more precisely the model is steered toward chemically or biologically meaningful outputs. For the metabolism example, the model receives the parent molecule and enzyme, then submits a predicted metabolite. The verifier compares the predicted and reference molecular fingerprints—numerical representations of structural features—using Tanimoto similarity. Tanimoto similarity is a metric used to measure the overlap between two sets or binary vectors and is calculated by dividing the size of their intersection by the size of their union. For the bit fingerprints used here, the score ranges from 0 to 1; higher scores indicate more similar fingerprints. Figure 2. The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL post-training workflow Direct RL post-training on the custom environment With the environment in place, fine-tune the model using group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with low rank adapters (LoRA). The environment presents the model with an experimental input and asks it to reason through the problem step-by-step before submitting a predicted answer via a tool call. Each submission is scored automatically by the verifier, giving a dense reward signal that requires no further annotation. The training loop, reward server, harness, and rollout workers are fully self-contained, so the same pipeline generalizes to any domain that can return a scalar reward. At a 16,384-token output budget on the drug-metabolism RLVR environment, supervised fine tuning (SFT) improved the accuracy of Nemotron for Science by 12% and RL post-trained lifted it a further 17%. It demonstrates that even a highly capable instruction-tuned model continues to improve meaningfully when given targeted RL feedback on a domain-specific task. Figure 3. This chart shows mean molecular similarity before and after post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. Distillation from stronger models as a “warm-start” for RL If the base model needs a capability boost before RL training or if RL convergence is slow, a distillation step can provide significant lift. A stronger teacher model (e.g. a larger frontier model or a specialist) is run against the same environment to generate high-quality reasoning traces. A reasoning trace is high quality if the teacher model’s step-by-step logic for identifying the enzyme, predicting the reaction site, and deriving the metabolite structure leads to a SMILES that matches the ground truth metabolite. It is a low-quality reasoning trace even if the reasoning looks fluent and plausible but has some flawed logic that resulted in the wrong prediction. The high-quality reasoning traces are used to fine-tune the student model via SFT or direct on-policy distillation, giving it a much better starting point before the RL loop begins. This is known as a “warm-start” and it typically accelerates convergence and raises the performance floor, making the subsequent RL training more efficient and more likely to find a strong policy. Data distillation for SFT The distillation pipeline runs Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 across the training set, scores each rollout by Tanimoto similarity (tool call) to the ground truth metabolite, and keeps only the (question, reasoning trace) pairs where the model got it right. Those become the SFT corpus for the smaller model. In this environment 1,123 high-quality reasoning traces were filtered from 1,934 training prompts at Tanimoto threshold ≥ 0.7. Here is a distilled reasoning trace for a question-answer pair from Claude Sonnet 5.5. Note that a fixed system prompt is included with every request, which can be varied across environments. LLM requests are formatted as chat messages containing both the question and the system prompt. MetxBioDB environment (CYP1A2 N-demethylation) Question: Parent compound SMILES: Cc1nn(C)c(Cl)c1C(O)=Nc1cccc2c1C(C)OC2(C)C Metabolising enzyme: CYP1A2 Reason through this biotransformation step by step, then call submit_metabolite with the predicted SMILES of the primary metabolite. Ground truth: Cc1[nH]nc(Cl)c1C(O)=Nc1cccc2c1C(C)OC2(C)C — Tanimoto similarity = 1.0 (exact match) System prompt: You are an expert computational chemist specializing in drug metabolism. Your task is to predict the SMILES string of the metabolite produced when a given parent compound is biotransformed by a specified enzyme or enzyme family. Response format: 1. Provide step-by-step scientific reasoning: a. Identify the functional groups in the parent compound relevant to the enzyme. b.

item.title: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Achieves up to 2x Blackwell Ultra Performance in MLPerf Training v6.1
item.abstract: As AI agents tackle increasingly complex workflows, reducing time-to-train is critical for rapidly iterating on both models and the agents they power. MLPerf Training v6.1 marks the debut of the NVIDIA Vera Rubin architecture, and these early results demonstrate that its CUDA software stack is already highly mature. In its first appearance, the Vera Rubin NVL72 platform delivered the fastest time to train on six of the seven benchmarks, achieving up to 2x more performance than a highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 baseline. For the seventh benchmark, DeepSeek-V3 671B, NVIDIA captured the absolute fastest time of the round by demonstrating massive scale on a 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 cluster. This dual-platform approach deliberately showcases the strengths of both systems. While the GB300 results highlight the massive, reliable cluster scale NVIDIA is deploying today, Vera Rubin demonstrated its own exceptional scaling architecture by maintaining above 97% overall efficiency when scaling from 256 to 1,024 GPUs. Together, NVIDIA platforms hold the fastest time to train on every benchmark in v6.1. NVIDIA platforms were also the only ones to submit results across all seven benchmarks, with Vera Rubin successfully completing the entire suite in its inaugural run. For developers, this breadth matters as much as any single top-line number. It proves that the performance gains inherited on day one span the entire modeling pipeline, comprehensively supporting everything from large-scale pretraining to the reinforcement learning post-training required for modern AI agents. Comprehensive AI performance across all MLPerf training benchmarks The simplest way to read this round is per benchmark: How much more performance does the new platform deliver per GPU on the same model? The suite covers natural language, image generation, recommendation, and reinforcement learning, so the gains hold across multiple modalities as well as across different model shapes and architectures. DeepSeek-V3 671B: 2x per GPU on the hardest workload DeepSeek-V3 671B is a 671-billion-parameter token-dropless Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model and the most demanding workload in the suite. Expert parallelism turns every iteration into a burst of all-to-all communication, so fabric efficiency shows up directly in time to train. Vera Rubin NVL72 trained the benchmark in 4.14 minutes using 1,024 GPUs across 16 racks. GB300 NVL72 ran the identical 1,024-GPU configuration in 8.03 minutes, close to 2x per GPU, and the largest generational improvement in this round. Halving time to train roughly doubles how many experiments a team can run in a quarter, and experiment throughput is what moves model quality. At a larger scale, GB300 NVL72 produced the fastest absolute result of the round: 1.38 minutes across 10,240 GPUs. That is one training job spread across 160 racks, each its own NVLink domain, and it shows the platform’s scale-out fabric holding up long after the job outgrows a single rack. Post-training arrives, and Vera Rubin leads it MLPerf Training v6.1 adds its first agentic LLM reinforcement learning post-training benchmark , Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO, reflecting a fundamental shift in AI development. Post-training has emerged as the critical differentiator for agentic accuracy, making the GRPO workload uniquely demanding. The continuous cycle of generating rollouts, scoring them, and updating weights pushes system architectures to their limits by forcing constant, massive weight migrations between inference and training engines. Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved the fastest time for this new benchmark with a time of 10.44 minutes at 1,024 GPUs (6.1-0117), compared with 13.78 minutes for GB300 NVL72 (6.1-0031) at the same scale. Teaching these models to observe, reason, and act requires running each rollout in a simulated environment and executing tool calls, code, or API validations. Because driving these simulations is intensely CPU-bound, the NVIDIA Vera CPU is integral to the architecture , sustaining more than 22,500 concurrent RL environments across 256 CPUs in a single Vera CPU rack. While the GPUs handle massive token generation and rapid weight updates, the Vera CPUs work in lockstep to simulate the environments, ensuring the accelerators are continuously fed with the rich feedback required to perfect agentic workflows. NVLink, Quantum-X and Spectrum-X: Co-designed networking for high-efficiency AI scaling Every result above is also a networking result. Modern AI training requires thousands of processors to act as one, a challenge NVIDIA solves by co-designing the internal rack domain and the external cluster fabric. Inside the rack, Vera Rubin NVL72 connects 72 GPUs and 36 CPUs through a copper NVLink 6 spine. Delivering 3.6 TB/s per GPU and 260 TB/s per rack, this all-to-all domain keeps MoE expert dispatch off the critical path. Beyond the rack, the platform scales out via ConnectX-9 SuperNICs over Quantum-X800 InfiniBand or Spectrum-X Ethernet. To manage bursty MoE traffic, both fabrics use adaptive routing and congestion control to keep all-to-all communications hidden behind the compute layer. This cohesive design translates directly to efficiency. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved above 97% scaling efficiency as it scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs (4 to 16 racks). GB300 NVL72 showcased the platform’s large-scale capabilities , extending to 10,240 GPUs to capture the fastest absolute result of the round. Because the NVL72 architecture provides a consistent 72-GPU domain, developers see predictable performance jumps every generation without altering their operating model. Each cycle simply delivers more compute and bandwidth across the same consistent fabric. Figure 2.

item.title: Taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns, anti-patterns, and lessons from manufacturing
item.abstract: Enterprise teams are building multi-agent systems, and when early implementations fall short, the cause is rarely the model. Multi-agent coordination is a distributed systems problem, and many teams taking it on haven’t yet built distributed systems instincts. The numbers are consistent across sources: ~88% of AI pilots never reach production . Stanford HAI demonstrated that two models can perform worse collaborating than either alone when coordination overhead exceeds the benefit. The pattern is clear: teams are adding complexity faster than they build understanding. Ten steps that are each 95 percent reliable deliver only 59.9 percent end-to-end reliability, and 20 steps deliver 35.8 percent. This illustrative model assumes a strictly sequential chain with no retries, but the direction holds: each dependent handoff multiplies risk. In this post, you learn how to decide whether a use case needs multiple agents, choose a coordination pattern, and spot costly anti-patterns early. You also see how takt time, safety boundaries, edge data, and shift cycles shape the architecture. Coordination patterns fall into two tiers, based on who controls the flow. In Tier 1, you define the path. In Tier 2, the model chooses the path at runtime. That flexibility handles work whose steps you can’t define in advance, at a higher cost in tokens, latency, and debugging. The practical default is to start with Tier 1 and move a task to Tier 2 only when its subtasks emerge during the work. 1.1 Sequential Pipeline: Orchestration patterns that implement linear execution where each node’s output feeds into the next node (A -> B -> C) supporting ordered processing with predictable execution timing In the following diagram, input flows to agent A (extract), then agent B (transform), then agent C (validate), and then output. The user defines that order at build time, and nothing is decided at runtime. As a result, the pipeline is straightforward to debug and test, and its cost is predictable. Typical fits include document processing, extract, transform, and load (ETL) chains, and warranty-claim triage. Figure 1: Sequential pipeline where each agent’s output feeds the next, from extract to transform to validate 1.2 Conditional Workflow: Logic-based edges select the next node by condition, so the workflow can branch and send each case down a different path. In the following diagram, a user request goes to agent A (write code) and then to agent B (test code). A pass/fail check sends passing work to agent D (deploy). Failing work loops back to agent A for a retry, up to a maximum of N times, and then escalates to a human. The orchestration layer enforces that cap, for example through an AWS Step Functions iteration limit, which keeps the loop from becoming the unbounded iteration anti-pattern described later in this post. Figure 2: Conditional workflow that retries failures up to N times before escalating to a human A classification step examines the input and directs it to the appropriate processing path. Only one path is executed per request. Best for intent-driven dispatch, quality-gate decisions, customer inquiry routing, and anomaly triage. The following diagram shows a plant supervisor’s request being read by a classifier and sent to exactly one specialist. Questions about whether parts meet spec go to the Quality Agent, overdue equipment services go to the Maintenance Agent, and shift changes go to the Scheduling Agent. This decision is made at the entry point. Figure 3: Conditional router that runs one path per request, with bounded retries before human escalation 1.4 Parallel Workflow: A task splits into independent subtasks that run simultaneously across handlers, each on its own data. A fan-in step combines the results when all handlers complete, and a failure in one path retries only that path. Best for multi-source analysis, batch processing, and work that decomposes into independent pieces. In the following diagram, a research orchestrator decomposes the task and dispatches it to three specialist agents that run concurrently: a financial data agent, a geopolitical agent, and a logistics agent, each analyzing its own source. A combined step waits for all three, then synthesizes the results, resolves conflicts, and ranks the findings. Latency equals the slowest single agent rather than the sum of all three. Figure 4: Parallel fan-out to specialist agents followed by a fan-in step that synthesizes and ranks the results In autonomous patterns, control flow is determined at runtime by the AI model itself, not predefined by developers. Agents read task state, reason about what’s needed and coordinate through shared context rather than fixed paths spanning a spectrum from structured orchestration to fully emergent behavior. In plan-based orchestration, a single orchestrator agent acts as a project manager. The orchestrator maintains an explicit task plan with assignments and dependencies, sees all context while each worker receives only its slice, distributes work dynamically against the current plan, and monitors progress centrally. Key design choice is that the workers are stateless and independent. If one fails, it doesn’t contaminate others. The orchestrator retries only the failed worker, not the entire workflow. The following diagram shows how a planner agent decomposes a task into an explicit plan and dispatches each step to a worker’s agent. Each step goes to a dedicated worker (a research agent, an analysis agent, and a report agent) that sees only its assigned slice. Figure 5: Plan-based orchestration with a planner agent assigning each step to a stateless worker agent Agents operate with limited, local knowledge and coordinate through peer-to-peer delegation. Each makes local decisions about when and to whom to transfer control, based on the task and the agents it knows. Control passes with state: each transfer carries validated task state, the evidence behind it, and any unresolved questions, so the receiving agent continues rather than reinterpreting a summary. A handoff that moves only through the conversation is not a handoff. In the following diagram, a customer service agent transfers control, together with its context, to either a technical support agent or a billing agent, and technical support can hand off further to a senior engineer. Each agent knows only the small set of peers it can transfer to. Figure 6: Handoff pattern passing validated state between peer agents through local delegation In conversation-driven patterns (also known as group chat patterns), all agents participate in a shared conversation where orchestration emerges through turn-taking rather than explicit plans or structured handoffs. This mirrors human team collaboration where everyone can see the discussion and contribute when appropriate. In the following diagram, an agent-selection mechanism decides whose turn it is, and agents A, B, and C each add to one shared conversation, where every turn is a message plus a tool call. The selection mechanism sets the turn-taking, and state lives implicitly in the conversation history. Figure 7: Conversation-driven pattern where turn-taking selects the next agent and state lives in the conversation Multiple agents independently evaluate the same input, and their conclusions are reconciled by majority, by a judge agent, or by escalation when they disagree. Unlike a conversation-driven pattern, the agents do not see each other’s reasoning before committing to a position, which is what makes disagreement informative rather than socially convergent. Use it sparingly. Debate is the most expensive pattern here, and on perceptual tasks it buys latency rather than accuracy (see the quality-inspection case in anti-pattern 3 that follows). Reserve it for high-stakes, low-volume decisions where being wrong costs more than deliberating.

item.title: Use prompt caching with open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock
item.abstract: Many generative AI applications send the same long context with every request, and prompt caching avoids processing it again each time. That context can be a system prompt, reference documents, tool definitions, or the conversation so far. Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock can reuse it across requests, which helps reduce input costs and response latency. Prompt caching reuses the computed state of a matching prompt prefix, so repeated context is read from cache instead of being processed again. Amazon Bedrock manages the cache for you. Depending on the model, you can use implicit caching, which works automatically, explicit caching, where you mark the reusable prefix, or both. The more context you reuse, and the more often you reuse it, the more you can save. As with other models on Amazon Bedrock, your prompts and outputs aren’t shared with the model provider or used to train models. For more information, see Data protection in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock now support explicit prompt caching. In this post, we use both modes with an open-weight model through the Chat Completions API and show how to read cache usage from each response. We then apply implicit caching to an OpenCode coding agent session on the same API and close with best practices. When a request starts with the same content as an earlier one, Amazon Bedrock reads that prefix from cache and processes only the rest. Cache reads are billed at a lower rate than standard input, so the savings can grow each time a prefix is reused. Depending on the model, cache writes can be billed at a higher rate than standard input. See Amazon Bedrock pricing for the rates of each model. Supported modes depend on the model and the API. For each model’s caching modes, minimum prefix length, and how long entries stay cached, see Models at a glance . The two modes compare as follows: Implicit caching : Amazon Bedrock reuses eligible prefixes automatically, on a best-effort basis. In a conversation, each request resends the full context, so the previous request becomes the cached prefix of the next one (Figure 1). As the prompt caching guide recommends, put static content first and dynamic content last. Keeping the start of the prompt stable lets every later request reuse it. If an early part changes, as in turn 4 of Figure 1, the cache is rebuilt from that point. Figure 1: Implicit prompt caching across the turns of a conversation Explicit caching : You mark the end of each reusable prefix with a cache breakpoint. You can add several breakpoints, up to the maximum that the model supports, to cache layers that change at different rates, as Figure 2 shows. Content up to each breakpoint is written to cache once and then read on later requests, and content after the last breakpoint is processed on each request. Check the model card for the minimum token count before a breakpoint, the maximum number of breakpoints, and the time to live (TTL), which resets with each cache hit. Figure 2: Explicit prompt caching with a breakpoint after the shared prefix With implicit caching, Amazon Bedrock can also write content to cache that later requests never reuse, such as a question that’s different each time. When the content after a shared prefix changes on every request, use explicit caching to limit cache writes to the shared prefix. Content after the last breakpoint is billed at the standard input rate. On models that charge more for cache writes, you don’t pay the higher write rate for content that’s never read back. Your use of the model is also subject to the AWS Responsible AI Policy . The example is a support assistant for a fictional water filter, the AnyCompany AquaPure 500. The system prompt holds a one-line instruction and the owner’s manual, which is the reusable prefix. Each request asks a different customer question. The samples use the OpenAI Python SDK with the Amazon Bedrock Chat Completions endpoint. For authentication, the provide_token() function from the aws-bedrock-token-generator package turns your AWS credentials into a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key , valid for up to 12 hours. item.title: Introducing the Databricks AI Index: The state of enterprise AI tokenomics
item.abstract: Developers have more AI models and coding agents to choose from than ever before. Since May 2026, a new flagship proprietary or open-weight model has launched roughly every week, or every 3.7 days when regional labs are included. With so many options, knowing which models perform best, what they cost, and when to switch is becoming harder. At Databricks, we have a unique perspective on this rapidly changing landscape. Thousands of enterprises use Unity Gateway to access and govern AI models, providing us with insights into real-world model adoption and spending. Databricks also heavily leverages AI internally across our 12,000+ employees, and we've invested substantial research in evaluating the quality and cost of new frontier models on enterprise tasks. Today, we're launching the Databricks AI Index , a public resource that brings these insights together. Customers have repeatedly asked us how new models compare and what we're seeing across enterprise AI adoption to help inform their own investments. Now, for the first time, we're making our internal evaluation suite permanently public, with weekly updates as we evaluate new proprietary and open-weight model releases. The Index combines two complementary sources of data: Enterprise AI usage and spending. Aggregated, anonymized data from 10,000+ companies using Unity Gateway , spanning digital natives, Fortune 500, and Global 2000 enterprises, including traffic to external providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI. The Index tracks model adoption through token and spend shares across proprietary and open-weight models, as well as weekly AI spending patterns for individual users. Continuously updated coding-agent evaluations. Building on the coding-agent benchmark we published in July , our latest evaluations draw on real coding-agent workflows from Databricks engineers, captured through Unity Gateway. These workflows span creating and reviewing pull requests, investigating issues, and tackling complex development tasks. Using tasks from our private codebase and withheld tests helps reduce the risk of benchmark contamination while enabling consistent comparisons of model-harness combinations and terms of task success rates and cost per completed task. Together, these data sources show which models enterprises are adopting, how well different combinations of models and harnesses perform, and what they cost. Here are some highlights: Enterprises are increasingly shifting workloads between model versions and providers. At mid-year, most organizations relied on a handful of Anthropic models for the majority of their work. Today, adoption is far more fragmented across model versions and providers alike. OpenAI's share of enterprise token traffic grew meaningfully over this period, driven largely by its 6 series Sol and Astra models. However, model quality continues to strongly influence provider market share; when Claude Opus 5.5 launched, momentum shifted back to Anthropic. In just six weeks, Opus 5.5 surged from 7.2% to 37.9% of proprietary-model tokens, lifting Anthropic's overall share from 57.6% to 68.8%. The pattern of shifting workloads between models and providers aggressively matches our own AI strategy at Databricks, where we quickly evaluate and roll out new models. Two months ago, we introduced an internal Day 1 model rollout process which lets us evaluate new releases within days. This process has helped us manage cost while increasing the quality of internal AI efforts. For example, we found Opus 5.5 delivered improved quality at 29% lower cost per session than its predecessor, helping inform our decision to make it the default model for Claude Code. Enterprises are increasingly moving beyond a single AI provider. As recent as July, approximately 64% of enterprises using Unity Gateway relied on just one model provider. By November 2, that had fallen to 28% as more organizations adopted models from more 2 or more providers. Open-weight models are gaining ground alongside this shift. Their share of enterprise token traffic grew from 7.3% in July to 30.9% in November, more than quadrupling in less than four months. Open-weight models are also becoming increasingly competitive with proprietary alternatives. In our coding quality benchmark, three open-weight models rank among the top 10, including DeepSeek V4.1 and GLM 5.3, which both rank third with a 93.1% pass rate. In our research on open-weight models, we find that their growing capabilities, cost efficiency, and flexibility are making them an increasingly attractive option for enterprises. Choosing the right coding agent means evaluating both the model and the harness running it. Our latest coding-agent benchmark evaluates models across nine AI labs using Claude Code and Codex. Five models from four labs (OpenAI, DeepSeek, Meta, and Anthropic) sit on the cost-quality frontier, delivering the best trade-offs between task success rates and cost. The results show why model rankings alone don't tell the full story. Enterprises need to evaluate model and harness combinations against their own workloads, using real usage data and traces to understand the trade-offs between performance and cost. We use this approach internally at Databricks. When evaluating whether to upgrade from Opus 4.8 to Opus 5, we analyzed the cost-quality Pareto frontier and replayed traces from our own workloads. The results showed the upgrade wasn't worth the additional cost for our use cases, so we decided to stay on 4.8. Two models can deliver nearly the same benchmark performance at dramatically different costs. In our coding benchmark, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5 both achieved an 89.1% task success rate. However, Luna averaged just $0.05 per task compared with $1.62 for Opus 5.5, a roughly 32x difference. Cost per task depends on both token prices and the amount of work a model must do to reach an answer. Extra turns, long outputs and failed attempts all increase cost. Gemini 3.8 Flash has a low token price, yet it averaged 140 turns per task and finished as one of the most expensive models in the benchmark at $11.97 per task. For coding agents, lower token prices don't guarantee lower costs when models require more work to complete a task. Higher benchmark performance often comes at a steep price, and even small improvements in quality can carry high costs. Claude Fable 5.1 tops our benchmark with a 96.0% task success rate at $7.47 per task, while Muse Wonder scores 94.9% at just $1.53. That additional 1.1 percentage points of performance comes at nearly five times the cost. Enterprises appear to agree, and we saw Fable 5.1's share of proprietary tokens fall from 5.5% to 0.6% over 6 weeks since its launch. The question for enterprises is how much additional quality a task actually requires. Premium models can be worth the cost for complex, high-stakes work, but less expensive alternatives may be sufficient for routine tasks. Intelligent model routing, such as Smart Routing in Unity Gateway, can help match tasks to appropriate models based on quality and cost. AI spending varies dramatically across enterprise users. A developer running coding agents throughout the day has very different consumption patterns from those of an employee who asks an AI assistant a few questions a day. Our data highlights the stark difference: the median user spent just $2.49 on AI, while the 99th-percentile user spent $699.74, roughly 281x more. Median weekly spending more than doubled from $1.10 over six weeks, while spending at the 90th and 99th percentile remained relatively flat. This suggests that AI consumption is growing among typical users, but a small group still accounts for most of the AI bill. For enterprises, the trend makes visibility into the distribution of spending especially important. Understanding those differences helps organizations set more targeted budgets and spend controls without unnecessarily restricting usage.
