item.title: How we make Together AI easy for coding agents to use
item.abstract: Earlier this year, we started seeing more and more devs using coding agents to build with Together AI. It’s not hard to see why: It might take days or even weeks for a developer to wire up an app for production inference by hand, especially if they’re new to the platform. But for an agent using our SDK and CLI, it only takes a few minutes—at least in theory. In practice, we had no idea whether the agents pointed at our platform were able to work with Together efficiently, or if they were hitting obstacles, going down rabbit holes or failing outright, and wasting tokens in the process. As devs delegate more of their work to agents, developer experience (DX) is increasingly becoming synonymous with agent experience (AX). The easier your software is for agents to use, the easier it is for devs to build it into their own products and workflows. GitHub is a textbook example of great AX: activity on the platform has tripled in the past year, with agents opening about 40% of all PRs in 2026 (and, we’re willing to bet, writing a lot more than 40% of the lines of code across all commits). This is thanks to GitHub’s phenomenal API, CLI, and docs, all of which make it exceptionally easy for agents to use. (This writer was not even aware GitHub had a CLI until agents started using it for him, and now he probably uses it 1000+ times a day). To improve our AX at Together AI, we needed a way to measure how agent-ready our platform actually was. In this post, we’ll walk through how we run agent evals, two problems they uncovered and how we fixed them, and what we’ve learned. How we run agent evals at Together Building the task list Before we could start evaluating, we needed to know what agents were actually being asked to do … so we could, y’know, figure out if they could do those things. We started building a list of common tasks that developers tackle on Together, like running a batch inference job, building a voice agent, or managing autoscaling for an inference endpoint. By task, we really just mean a prompt, something you’d tell an agent to do—for example: List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it. To pass the eval, the agent has to: Find the latest pricing info. Call the regions API endpoint to list the available regions. Combine the two to find the cheapest option. Produce a valid CLI command for creating the cluster. The prompt asks for both availability and pricing, without mentioning that these details live in two different places. This is realistic, as the average user probably doesn’t know up front where each piece of information lives, which could easily trip up both humans and agents. Three configurations After building our list of tasks, we run each one of them three ways: Baseline: The agent receives just the prompt, with no special configuration, mirroring the average developer's workflow. It can use all its default tools, like fetching docs from the web, but we don't give it any specific MCP connectors or skills. MCP: The agent gets direct access to our documentation through our MCP server, so it knows exactly where to search when it hits a roadblock. Skills: We give the agent the Together skill package , which contains instructions and examples for using our services, written specifically for agents. The run matrix Each full evaluation runs every task against each agent configuration using three models, with two attempts at each task—so six attempts per task for each config, as shown here for our run on September 30th: gents passed 192 of 215 scored runs. The GPU cluster task failed every baseline run and passed every skills run. Automating the runs When we started building our evals, we ran everything by hand: open a new terminal, paste a prompt into Claude Code, let the agent do its thing (or fail to do its thing), and repeat for each configuration. It was manual and tedious, so once we figured out the shape of the system we wanted, we started automating it. Now we run each agent in a Together sandbox so they don’t interfere with our local environment or each other. GitHub Actions handles setup, starts the agent, cleans up afterward, and saves the results, while a proxy handles the agent's requests to the Together API and records the activity, so we can see which endpoints the agent calls and what comes back. Scoring a run After a run finishes, an LLM judge reviews the task prompt and the recorded session, then assigns one of three verdicts: Pass: Every task requirement was met. Incomplete: The agent attempted the task, but some required steps were unfinished or unverified. Fail: The agent gave up early, broke an explicit constraint, or produced an incorrect result (RIP). Failed and incomplete verdicts don’t necessarily tell us whether the problem was with the agent, the API, or missing evidence. They just tell us where to start looking. We investigate passing runs too. An agent can often work around confusing responses and still finish, and those recoveries show us what to fix to improve token efficiency. To make that review practical, we built a results viewer that compares how different models and configs performed. For each run, it shows the prompt, the tools the agent used, the responses it got back, and any API activity: Our results viewer comparing setups on the GPU cluster task. Both guided setups passed, and the skills runs used the fewest tool calls and cost the least. Case study 1: GPU cluster pricing Remember the GPU cluster task from earlier? List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it. Seems pretty simple, but when we ran our evals early last summer, Sonnet 4.6 passed only 4 of 15 attempts at this task, even with skills enabled. Our post-mortem revealed the same pattern in the failed runs: Sonnet treated the sample output in our CLI reference, which listed a single region and two GPU types, as if it were the live inventory. It also skipped the regions lookup and named what it thought was the cheapest option without ever checking the pricing page. The problems were on our end. First, the sample output wasn’t properly labeled, so nothing told the agent to run the command to retrieve the relevant data. Second, our skill file linked to the GPU clusters marketing page rather than the pricing table, so Sonnet opened the marketing page, didn’t see any real prices, and just made a best-effort guess at the cheapest GPU available. More capable models were able to work around the issue. In that same period, Opus 4.8 passed 13 of 14 attempts using the same config. According to the transcript, it noticed that the list_regions response didn't include prices, so it kept searching until it found them in our docs. This is why it’s crucial to test your product with less capable models; if we had only tested with Opus, it would have taken us much longer to find the gap. Isolating the failure To fix it, we isolated the failure by pulling the GPU clusters skill out of the full skill package, and wrote a narrower prompt that reproduced only this issue. It failed every time when tested against the old skill file, so we had reliable repro steps (use the old skill), and an easy way to test each new version (update the skill). We went through several iterations until we landed on a small change: two new sentences in the skill that point the agent to the pricing table, and explain how to use it with the live regions API: Query GET <https://api.together.ai/v1/compute/regions > or run tg clusters list-regions --json for the live region inventory, supported instance types, and compatible CUDA/driver pairs. Open the GPU Cluster pricing table for current on-demand and reserved rates.

item.title: Get answers from tables with tabular search in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
item.abstract: Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports tabular search, so you can get answers from tables through agentic retrieval. When a question needs data from CSV, XLSX, or XLS files, tabular search looks up values and runs calculations across every relevant row in one or more tables or sheets. It then combines the results with facts from related documents to answer analytical questions that take several steps. A finance team closing the quarter needs to know “Which departments must write variance commentary?” No single file has the answer. It depends on the variance policy’s threshold, the quarter-close memo’s budget revisions, and math over every department in the profit and loss (P&L) workbook. Like this finance team, most teams keep their narratives and data in the same place. For example, a Microsoft SharePoint site holds workbooks next to policies, and an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket holds CSV exports next to PDFs. Tabular search answers questions across these files through the same AgenticRetrieveStream request you already use for documents. It runs code over the original file in an isolated sandbox, so the answer uses the whole table instead of only the rows that retrieval returns. For the finance team, one request returns the departments that must write commentary. The answer cites the policy and the memo, and the trace names the workbook the code read. In this post, you learn how tabular search answers questions that need both table data and facts from documents, and when another tool is a better fit. You also build a knowledge base with sample finance files and use the trace to see which file the code read. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) returns a fixed number of passages that best match a question, which works well for prose. Tables lose information when they’re split into passages, in ways that depend on the table’s shape: Retrieval also has to match a question to the right table. Questions use business terms, such as “controllable spend,” but tables hold cost center codes, account names, and numbers. A draft and a final workbook look almost the same to search. The rule that gives the numbers meaning is often in a separate document, such as a policy. Tabular search therefore splits the work. Retrieval only has to return one passage from the right table file, and code then reads the whole table. Because retrieval still has to find that file first, naming the file in your question helps. Table 1 shows how plain retrieval and tabular search each handle the finance team’s question, “Which departments must write variance commentary?” Table 1: The same question with plain retrieval and with tabular search. In agentic retrieval , an agent uses retrieval to decide which documents matter and then writes the answer. Tabular search is part of that flow, so there’s nothing to turn on. When a question needs the data in a table, the request moves through these stages: Tabular search starts when retrieved passages come from a CSV, XLSX, or XLS file and the question needs a calculation across rows or a lookup of specific values. An AgenticRetrieveStream request can search one knowledge base or several. The Retrieve API keeps returning passages and doesn’t run code. Tabular search works the same way whichever connector brings the files into the knowledge base, including Amazon S3, Microsoft SharePoint, Atlassian Confluence, and others. Tabular search is built for questions that need calculations or lookups over the table files it retrieves. Running code adds at least one more agent turn, so answers that use table data take longer than text-only answers. Governed metrics, recurring dashboards, warehouse-scale joins, and reporting controls still belong in your business intelligence (BI) tools. Tabular search works on table files stored next to your documents, and you don’t define a schema. In this solution, an Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base stores your CSV and Excel files together with related documents, such as PDF and Word files. Your application sends every question through agentic retrieval. When a question needs table data, the answer combines calculations over your tables with facts from your documents. It cites the passages it used, and the trace names the table files the code read. When your application sends a question with AgenticRetrieveStream , agentic retrieval plans the work and retrieves passages from the knowledge base. If the question needs data from a table file, it sends the files to read to an isolated sandbox with no network access. There, model-written code runs over the original file and returns printed results. The answer, with citations and trace events, streams back to your application. The worked example uses fictitious AnyCompany Retail finance files: These files are in the tabular-search folder of the sample-managed-knowledge-base-patterns GitHub repository. item.title: Tabular foundation models on Databricks AI Runtime
item.abstract: Many of the most valuable predictive machine learning applications rely on tabular data. From credit risk and customer churn to demand forecasting and predictive maintenance, these use cases have traditionally required teams to develop, train and maintain models for each prediction task. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) offer another approach: pretrained models that can make predictions on new datasets without task-specific training. Productionizing ML systems at scale remains a challenge for many enterprises for the following reasons: Recently, agentic solutions have helped accelerate these expensive operations, but they still rely on a bespoke-trained model for each ML task or dataset. To remove this dependency, pioneering research labs have applied the transformer architecture to tabular data at scale, creating a new category of models called Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs). Because TFMs come pretrained, they require no training on your dataset, meaning bespoke training and retraining pipelines largely disappear. Despite the impressive accuracy these models demonstrate on public benchmarks, they have not yet cracked into the mainstream of enterprise AI. This is partially due to the nascent nature of the field, as not many practitioners know about them yet, but also due to compute infrastructure requirements. In this article, we'll examine how TFMs work, compare recent models and explain the trade-offs involved in adopting them for enterprise ML. We'll then demonstrate how Databricks AI Runtime supports TFM experimentation and fine-tuning with managed GPU infrastructure, integrated development tools and model governance. TFMs largely eliminate the need for training and the overhead of maintaining bespoke models. They are pretrained on millions of diverse synthetic datasets so that they can infer relationships between variables in an unseen dataset. At prediction time, the labeled rows are passed as context alongside the rows to predict. Attention, the core of the transformer architecture, then relates each new row to those examples. Predictions are produced by a single forward pass, a process called in-context learning (ICL). While this zero-shot approach provides a powerful baseline out of the box, TFMs can also be fine-tuned. By updating the model's pretrained weights on a specific dataset, ML teams can push predictive accuracy even higher for their most critical use cases. The main complexity for transformers in TFMs is handling various input types. Unlike words in text or pixels in an image, a table mixes numerical, categorical, and boolean features, each with its own scale and meaning. Efficiently embedding these inputs into a common latent space has been a major challenge. The community solved this by developing specialized tokenizers that map both categorical and numerical features into a single, shared representation. Once an efficient tokenization for every cell had been achieved, the problem was how to effectively learn the relationship between rows and columns. TabPFNv2 was the first to make this work at foundation-model scale. As shown in Figure 1, it involved applying attention mechanisms sequentially within rows and then within columns, capturing the complex interactions between features and the underlying relationships across different data samples. Despite its success, this approach faces severe scalability limits. By performing dense attention across rows and then columns, the computational cost grows rapidly, making it prohibitively expensive as the number of samples and features increases. As a solution, TabICLv1 uses a row-compression approach, in which specialized encoders represent each row with just four tokens, making attention across samples much cheaper while maintaining competitive predictive performance. This architecture is shown in Figure 2, but it has since been adopted and extended by models like TabPFNv3 , TabFM , and KumoTabular , which are among the top-ranked models in benchmarks like TabArena today. Apart from the architecture, another distinctive feature of TFMs is how they are built: model creators primarily use synthetic data during the pretraining phase. The determining factor in a TFM's out-of-the-box success is whether these researchers can generate synthetic data that accurately represents the distributions and relationships of real-world datasets. To build a robust foundation model, creators must simulate large-scale, diverse data that captures common enterprise quality issues like missingness, outliers, and unobserved features. While Structural Causal Models provide a standardized framework for sampling these pretraining datasets, the exact pipeline configuration depends heavily on the specific TFM. As the TFM landscape rapidly evolves with frequent new releases, evaluating options for enterprise deployment requires careful scrutiny. The following table highlights leading models through the lens of two practical deployment factors: scale and licensing. For an exhaustive list of the current state of the art, check benchmarks like TabArena or TALENT . Given the unique trade-offs of each TFM, we recommend evaluating these models directly against your organization's data, as proprietary enterprise workloads often differ drastically from synthetic data or standard benchmarks. Beyond just measuring predictive accuracy, teams must also evaluate the operational cost. While TFMs save massive amounts of engineering time by eliminating bespoke training pipelines, running a foundation model on GPUs inherently costs more per prediction than executing a traditional XGBoost model on a CPU. For any given use case, evaluating a TFM means weighing that accelerated time-to-market and performance lift against the ongoing cost of GPU inference. Inference with TFMs is optimized on GPUs. The models themselves are small enough to fit on a single GPU, but with in-context learning, the entire training set is passed to the model with every prediction. As a result, GPU memory usage grows with the number of rows and features, and can quickly be exhausted at the dataset sizes typical of enterprise ML. The need for a performant GPU leads to three problems: Databricks unifies data and AI in a single open platform. AI Runtime, a fully managed serverless GPU infrastructure, offers this unified experience for enterprise GPU workloads. Experimentation and productionization have never been easier using AI Runtime, which includes features such as: With Databricks AI Runtime, you can run your TFM workloads right where your data lives, using Unity Catalog to govern and manage the lifecycle of your GPU workflows without creating any silos. Clone this repository to see how to run zero-shot inference with various TFMs using Databricks AI Runtime, alongside complete fine-tuning examples for classification and regression with KumoTabular. These examples showcase how AI Runtime helps you easily manage the lifecycle and integration of advanced TFM fine-tuning workflows. Video 2 walks through the fine-tuning notebook with an H100, showing how GPU usage observability is embedded right into the notebook as well as the MLflow experiment used for metric tracking. Additionally, the workflow covers centralized governance and registration through Unity Catalog, facilitating robust version control and structured model lifecycle management. Tabular foundation models promise to reduce the time to market of ML initiatives from months to days, and with Databricks AI Runtime, GPU workloads are no longer an obstacle.

item.title: Hark Releases Handoff², a 2x Faster Computer-Use Agent for Hark Pro
item.abstract: Hark has released Handoff² , the second version of the computer-use agent inside its Hark Pro app. The Hark Handoff 2 computer-use agent finishes web tasks about 2x faster than the original, on average. Hark states that the gains come from reinforcement learning (RL) that penalized wasted turns and latency. For teams building browser agents, it is a case study in training for speed, not only accuracy. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Handoff² is a computer-use agent from Hark that operates websites the way a person does. It clicks, types and scrolls on live pages instead of calling APIs. Hark previewed Handoff in August and shipped it in Hark Pro in October. Since then, Hark says it has logged over 5.6M browsing sessions and handled over $20M in purchases. Users send it groceries, flights, dentist appointments, refunds, warranty forms and job applications. Hark co-evolved 2 things: the agent harness and the RL training recipe. The new harness lets the model emit more actions per turn. Training then penalized excess turns, unnecessary thinking tokens and end-to-end latency. item.title: OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion
item.abstract: OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing. OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI. The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic , which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat. The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user. Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions. Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company. Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers. With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI. Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organization is also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release. At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits. Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations. Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work. Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged. In previous coverage, John Steidley, chief of staff at Palisade Research, told TechCrunch that it’s important to see this data in order to assess whether a model was trained to perform well on a “shutdown resistance benchmark.” In OpenAI’s first pilot, the AI lab is providing Apollo with access to only the information required to assess whether the models engage in subversion attempts. This includes “relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints.” The scope of access will be limited to “only the agreed claims and only for the specific models and time periods agreed for the assessment,” Apollo says. OpenAI still reserves the right to withhold certain information within that scope if it deems it necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks, or IP protection. The company agreed not to withhold information simply because it is unfavorable. Apollo also won’t get access to all OpenAI staffers, instead being limited to “only authorized staff,” which are participants that the AI lab selects, though Apollo can suggest certain individuals. Crucially, if an OpenAI employee outside this group raises confidential information within the scope of Apollo’s research, the firm cannot follow up and will need to cease communication and route follow-up through OpenAI. That condition is significant. It comes in the wake of OpenAI firing three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential information with safety evaluation firm METR — which performed the Hugging Face incident post-mortem alongside independent AI safety research group Redwood. Buck Shlegeris, CEO of Redwood, said in a post on Monday that the agreements announced don’t meet the bar of granting third parties “employee-like access,” saying it’s “disappointing but not surprising.” OpenAI said that they'd have embedded evaluations with employee-like access; the agreements announced today obviously don't meet that bar. This is disappointing but not surprising. Maybe future agreements will be better. https://t.co/kmDbg1Dqav — Buck Shlegeris (@bshlgrs) November 16, 2026 The pilot will also be limited in how much researchers can disclose. While Apollo will be allowed to publish independent conclusions of its findings, OpenAI will be able to limit evidence available to substantiate them publicly, which could make it hard for outsiders to independently assess the findings. Apollo has pushed back against this limitation, saying it believes researchers should be allowed to disclose the findings of the evaluation “to an appropriate outside audience even if the developer was trying to prevent the disclosure of unfavorable findings.” That said, while the public cannot see the full supporting evidence, OpenAI says its Safety and Security Committee, which oversees safety on behalf of the OpenAI Foundation’s board, will get to review unredacted assessment reports and can communicate privately with evaluators.
